title: WPMS/14/2015 of Kurdi AND OTHERS Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 14 of 2015
Kurdi & Others ...Petitioners

Versus
State of Uttarakhand & Others ...Respondents
Present: Mr. Jitendra Chaudhary, Advocat for the petitioners.
 Mr. R.C. Arya, Standing Counsel along with Mr. Tarun
Lakhera, Brief Holder for the State /respondent No. 1.
 Mr. Sanjay Kumar, Advocate holding brief of Mr. Tapan
Singh, Advocate for the respondent No. 2
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J. (Oral)
 Under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition
and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (in short U.P.Z.A & L.R. Act),
the classification of tenure-holders has been given under
Section 129. Section 129 of the Act in its sub Section (3)
deals with the terms "asami". A vivid description about the
liabilities and rights of an "asami" has been dealt with
under Section 133 of the Act, which reads as under:-
"133. Asami. - Every person belonging to any of the
following classes shall be called an asami and shall
have all the rights and be subject to all the liabilities
conferred or imposed upon asami by or under this Act,
namely -
[(a) every person who, as a consequence of the
acquisition of estates, becomes an asami under
Section 11, 13 or 21;]
[(b) every person, who was admitted before the
commencement of the Uttar Pradesh Land Laws
(Amendment) Act, 1977 by a bhumidhar or sirdar
or after such commencement, by a bhumidhar as
a lessee of land comprised in his holding, in
accordance with the provisions of this Act;]

2
(c) every person who, on or after the date of vesting,
is admitted by the [Land Management
Committee] or the person entitled as a lessee of
land described in Section 132; and
[(d) every person who in any other manner acquires
the rights of an asami under or in accordance
with the provisions of this Act or of any other law
for the time being in force.]"
2. Under sub Section (c) of Section 133 of the Act,
it confers the right on the Land Management Committee to
enter a person entitled to have a land as a lessee on a
land, which is vested in Gaon Sabha. Meaning thereby for
all practical purposes, since it is an admitted case of the
petitioner that he is an asami pattedar, he would be falling
to be as "asami" as described under Section 133 of the
U.P.Z.A. & L.R. Act.
3. According to the petitioner himself, he was
allotted a land in 1984-85 lying in khata No. 135 khasra
No. 145(145/1 to 145/6) having an area of 0.629 hectares
out of which the land which was allotted to the petitioner
falls to be in khasra No. 145/1 having an area of 0.097
hectares falling in category '3' land.
2. Once the petitioner admits the fact that he is an
asami pattedar, the consequential effect would be that his
rights would be regulated by Rule 176-A which deals with
the "asami pattedars" and under the proviso to Rule 176-A,
such "asami pattedar" will have a right to continue to
occupy the land, thus allotted to him by the Land

3
Management Committee only for a period of five years.
The proviso to Rule 176-A reads as under :-
"Provided that no lease shall be made to an asami for a
period exceeding five years."
3. On a simple interpretation of the intention of the
proviso is that it creates a restriction that under no set of
circumstances, an asami lease granted in favour of a
person is entitled to be granted an asami patta can be for
a period more than five years from the date of grant. The
contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that
after the land having been allotted to his father (though no
such lease has been brought on record by the petitioner to
show whether it was actually in existence or not and what
its length of period). The basic rights which he now
stresses upon which he contends to be flowing to him from
the patta executed in favour of his father in 1984-85 is that
the allotment now which has been made to respondent No.
3 for opening of a school is bad for the reason;
(i) The asami patta executed in his favour was never
cancelled, and;
(ii) No show-cause notice was issued to the petitioner
prior to the allotment made by the Land Management
Committee to respondent No. 3 for opening of a
school was without hearing the petitioner.
4. He questions the allotment made in favour of the
respondent No. 3 on the ground that for the purpose of

4
making an allotment there has had to be fulfillment of
contentions contemplated under Section 195 of the
U.P.Z.A & L.R. Act. That means it has to be a vacant land.
He contends that since patta continued in his favour it
would be presumed that he is in possession and once he
is continuing in possession no allotment could have been
made to respondent No. 3 for opening of the school.
5. To support his contention, he places on record a
copy of the khataunis and jodhbahi to show that he is in
possession. I am afraid to accept the contention because
these two documents under revenue law can never be a
document which is admissible as a proof of evidence for
the purposes of substantiating the possession. Besides
this, even in the finding recorded by the impugned order
under challenge shows that the land was vacant at the
time when it was allotted to the respondent No. 3 for
running the school.
6. It is an admitted case further that the Gaon
Sabha has initiated the proceedings under Section 202 of
the U.P.Z.A. & L.R. Act for seeking eviction of the
petitioner, who claims himself to be an asami pattedar.
The proceedings thus drawn under Section 202 of the
U.P.Z.A. & L.R Act was registered as Revenue Case No.
244 of 2002, before the Court of Assistant Collector, which
was based upon a report of the Tehsildar dated
02.03.2001, wherein too in the report of the Tehsildar it
was recorded that the petitioner is not in possession.

5
However, the order of the Assistant Collector was put to
challenge in a revision preferred by the petitioner being
Revision No. 31 of 2002-03. The said revision, according
to the petitioner, has been allowed on 22.11.2002 and the
matter has been remitted back to the Assistant Collector
for re-deciding the issue under Section 202 of the U.P.Z.A.
& L.R. Act.
7. None of the parties to the writ petition are in a
position to address this Court as to what was the
consequence to the proceedings under Section 202 of the
Act after its remand made by the order dated 22.11.2002.
But rather on the other hand, the learned counsel for the
petitioner submits that though the proceedings under
Section 202 of the U.P.Z.A. & L.R. Act after remand was
pending, during the intervening period yet the Land
Management Committee passed a Resolution No. 4 on
26.08.2004, whereby the Land Management Committee
has allotted the land to respondent No. 3 for opening of a
school.
8. Even as per the Resolution dated 26.08.2004
(annexure 6 to the writ petition) a conscious decision was
taken by the Land Management Committee that the land at
the time when the allotment proposal was being
considered, it was held out to be a vacant land.
Accordingly, by the order of Assistant Collector dated
01.01.2005, it was allotted by the Land Management
Committee to respondent No. 3 holding thereof that it is

6
vacant/plain land and it would be most suitable place for
opening of a school, which would be meeting much wider
necessity of the people of village for imparting education to
the children of the village itself.
9. This order of allotment dated 01.01.2005 as
passed by the Assistant Collector too has recorded a
finding pertaining to the impact of Rule 176-A, on the
provisions of asami patta executed in favour of the
petitioner. This order was put to challenge in a revision by
the petitioner being Revision No. 3 of 2014-15. The
Revision too has been dismissed by the judgment and
order dated 26.12.2014.
10. According to the findings recorded by the
Revisional Court also it has been found that the land was
vacant and according to the reports submitted by the
Tehsildar after allotment being made on 01.01.2005, the
construction of the school, which was for a public purpose
was already proceeding with, meaning thereby findings
shows that the petitioner is not in possession as per the
legal consequences also due to Rule 176-A.
11. On account of the fact that the patta executed in
favour of the father of the petitioner has attained its legal
death, no right whatsoever would accrue to the petitioner,
in any manner entitling him to challenge the allotment
made in favour of the respondent No. 3. Hence the writ
petition fails and is accordingly dismissed. This Court does

7
not find any infirmity in the impugned orders dated
26.12.2014 passed by the Additional Commissioner,
Garhwal Mandal, Pauri in Revenue Revision No. 3 of
2014-15 "Sri Kurdi & others Vs. State of Uttarakhand and
others" as well as in the judgment and order dated
01.01.2005 passed by the Assistant Collector, 1st
Class/S.D.M, Laksar in Revenue Case No. 06 of 2004
"L.M.C. Vs. Junior High School". The two orders impugned
are hereby affirmed. Writ petition is dismissed. No order as
to costs.
